notes: TPO confirmation quashed for misleading officer report; costs ordered to detailed assessment.

enrichment.short_title: Gilman v Rutland: misleading TPO report and section 288 planning appeal
key_facts: Rutland County Council confirmed a provisional Tree Preservation Order over four trees in Mr Gilman's garden after a neighbour raised concerns linked to his redevelopment application.
Mr Gilman's planning application expressly stated that no trees would be affected and he had planted three of the trees to mark his children's births.
The officer report to committee wrongly implied that unless the order was confirmed the trees would be felled, despite no such intention being established.
Outline planning permission was later granted with a condition protecting the trees, but the committee confirmation was quashed on procedural fairness grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 appeal to the High Court against confirmation of a Tree Preservation Order.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed and the TPO confirmation quashed; the committee must reconsider on a fair report; costs awarded to the appellant subject to detailed assessment after summary assessment was declined.
enrichment.ratio: A planning committee report must fairly explain why a Tree Preservation Order is expedient in the interests of amenity; framing the choice as confirm the order or allow the trees to be felled when felling was not proposed is misleading and vitiates the decision.
legal_issues: Whether the officer report adequately reflected section 198(1) and the need for expediency in the interests of amenity
Whether misleading conclusions that the trees would be felled unless the order was made invalidated the committee's decision
Whether the committee could be assumed to have reached the same decision if properly informed
Whether human rights balancing required explicit reference in the report

confidence.notes: Collins J's findings on the misleading report and quashing order are clear and fully reasoned.

notes: Divisional Court declaration on Schedule 22 oral hearings for existing life prisoners' minimum terms.

enrichment.short_title: Hammond: Article 6 and oral hearings for existing life prisoners' tariffs
key_facts: The claimant was convicted of murdering a 13-month-old child and received mandatory life imprisonment before his tariff had been fixed by the Home Secretary.
Schedule 22 to the Criminal Justice Act 2003 required his case to be referred to a single High Court judge to fix the minimum term without an oral hearing.
He sought an oral hearing to give evidence on sexual abuse, motive and loss of control issues relevant to the minimum term.
The Home Secretary accepted an oral hearing might sometimes be required but argued Article 6 was satisfied by the Court of Appeal procedure as a whole.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review challenge by an existing mandatory life prisoner to paragraph 11 of Schedule 22.
enrichment.outcome: Declaration granted that paragraph 11 must be read subject to an implied discretion allowing the High Court judge to order an oral hearing where necessary for Article 6(1); guidance given on when hearings will be rare.
enrichment.ratio: Section 3 HRA requires primary legislation to be read compatibly with Convention rights at first instance; where an oral hearing is necessary under Article 6, a later compliant appeal does not render the High Court stage compatible or excuse reading paragraph 11 to permit discretion.
legal_issues: Whether paragraph 11 of Schedule 22 is incompatible with Article 6(1) in all cases
Whether non-compliance at first instance can be cured by the Court of Appeal procedure
The effect of De Cubber, Göç v Turkey and Findlay v UK on systemic versus casual Article 6 failures
How existing prisoners' minimum term references should be conducted in practice
linked_authorities: R (Anderson) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2002] UKHL 46
De Cubber v Belgium (1984) 7 EHRR 236
Göç v Turkey (2002) 34 EHRR 36

confidence.notes: Detailed Divisional Court judgment with clear declaration and procedural guidance.

notes: Proprietary estoppel compensation set aside; possession declaration modified to run until farm disposal.

enrichment.short_title: Wormall v Wormall: proprietary estoppel compensation beyond minimum equity
key_facts: Robert Wormall sought possession of Ibstock Grange Farm land used by his daughter Jill for an equestrian business she had built up with his encouragement over many years.

The recorder found proprietary estoppel entitling Jill to remain until six months after ancillary relief proceedings or 12 months, whichever was sooner, but also awarded £50,000 relocation compensation.
The judge found Jill reasonably expected to use the land while it remained in family ownership, not indefinitely regardless of events.
Robert appealed the compensation award; Jill did not cross-appeal the estoppel declaration.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission from Leicester County Court proprietary estoppel and possession proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the £50,000 compensation order set aside as wrong in principle; declaration modified so Jill may remain until completion of any disposal of the farm following ancillary relief.
enrichment.ratio: Once the equity is satisfied by a declaration giving effect to the expectation found (occupation while the farm remained family property), there is no further outstanding equity to justify additional compensation for an earlier departure caused by parental divorce rather than the promisor's assurances.
legal_issues: Whether compensation for early departure can be awarded after the minimum equity has been satisfied by a possession declaration
The scope of Jill's reasonable expectation based on Robert's encouragement
Whether the recorder erred by compensating for the breakdown of the parents' marriage
The appropriate form of declaration and possession timing pending ancillary relief
linked_authorities: Gillett v Holt [2001] Ch 210
Jennings v Rice [2003] 1 P&CR 100
Crabb v Arun District Council [1976] Ch 179

confidence.notes: Court of Appeal analysis of recorder's reasoning and compensation principle is explicit.

notes: Commercial Court appeal dismissed on Art 37.2 mitigation construction and fact findings.

enrichment.short_title: Sembawang v Pacific Ocean: contractual duty to mitigate completion costs
key_facts: Owners terminated a Singapore ship conversion contract under Article 37.1(e) and completed the work at Swan Hunter in the UK rather than local Singapore yards.
Article 37.2(b) required the builder to pay completion costs exceeding the contract price and stated that the owner has the duty to mitigate costs.
Arbitrators held owners' duty matched the common law mitigation standard of reasonableness and found no breach on the facts, including Keppel's lack of enthusiasm.
The yard appealed the tenth interim award on construction and breach of the mitigation duty.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court appeal with permission from a tenth interim arbitration award under the Arbitration Acts 1950–1979.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; arbitrators correctly construed the duty as requiring reasonable steps to mitigate and did not err in law in finding owners had not breached it.
enrichment.ratio: Duty to mitigate costs in Article 37.2(b) is a term of art importing the familiar common law standard of reasonableness, not an absolute duty to choose the cheapest yard regardless of commercial and arbitral considerations; whether mitigation was reasonable is primarily a question of fact.
legal_issues: Whether owners' duty to mitigate under Article 37.2(b) is absolute or corresponds to common law reasonableness
Whether termination without repudiatory breach alters the mitigation standard
Whether owners could consider arbitration access to records and commercial interests when choosing a completion yard
Whether the arbitrators erred in their findings on Keppel and Jurong
linked_authorities: Glencore Grain Rotterdam BV v Agros Trading Co Ltd [1999] 2 All ER 288
Payzu v Saunders [1919] 2 KB 581
The Solholt [1983] 1 Lloyd's Rep 605

confidence.notes: Long judgment but construction and breach conclusions are clearly stated.

notes: Al Fayed wrongful arrest appeal dismissed; Castorina and PACE reasonableness upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Al Fayed v Met Police: wrongful arrest and PACE detention at Kennington
key_facts: Mohamed Al Fayed and four Harrods employees were arrested at Kennington Police Station in March 1998 on suspicion of theft and criminal damage to contents of Tiny Rowland's safe deposit box.
Each had attended voluntarily by arrangement for interview; detention lasted only until interview concluded (up to 54 minutes) before release on bail.
Police investigation showed repeated unauthorised openings of the box by insiders in December 1995 and missing gems reported in June 1997.
Cresswell J dismissed claims for wrongful arrest and false imprisonment; the Court of Appeal upheld his reasoning on all grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Cresswell J's dismissal of damages claims for wrongful arrest and false imprisonment.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed; arresting officers had reasonable grounds for suspicion and exercised discretion Wednesbury reasonably; custody officers lawfully authorised brief detention for interview; indemnity costs ordered.
enrichment.ratio: Reasonable suspicion under section 24(6) PACE is conjecture or surmise where proof is lacking, not prima facie proof; joint enterprise opportunity evidence may support suspicion of multiple insiders; arrest for station interview can be Wednesbury reasonable despite voluntary attendance offers.
legal_issues: Whether arresting officers had reasonable grounds to suspect each appellant under section 24(6)
Whether arrest was Wednesbury unreasonable given voluntary attendance and cooperation
Whether custody officers had reasonable grounds under section 37(2)-(3) to detain for interview
Effect of Article 5 and post-HRA scrutiny on Castorina discretion
index_terms: Castorina v Chief Constable of Surrey
linked_authorities: Castorina v Chief Constable of Surrey [1996] LGR 241
Hussein v Chong Fook Kam [1970] AC 942
O'Hara v Chief Constable of the RUC [1997] AC 286
Cumming v Chief Constable of Northumbria [2003] EWCA Civ 1844

notes: Fact-finding that father caused fatal and prior non-accidental injuries; threshold passed for BL not S care order.

enrichment.short_title: Hampshire CC v SL: fact-finding on infant non-accidental injury and care orders
key_facts: Baby C died in December 2001 after collapse while being fed by her father DL; extensive fractures, retinal and subdural haemorrhages indicated repeated non-accidental injury.
DL was acquitted of murder and GBH at criminal trial but the family court conducted a fact-finding on the balance of probabilities.
Brothers S (8) and BL (2) remained with the mother under local authority proceedings; parents accepted a care order for BL but disputed one for S.
The judge found DL caused the fatal 2 December injury and earlier inflicted injuries; the mother was not culpable but had been uncooperative with social services.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court fact-finding and threshold hearing in public law care proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Threshold criteria satisfied for both children; care order approved for BL to remain with mother; no care order for S as intrusive and unnecessary given BL's order; father identified as risk requiring therapeutic work.
enrichment.ratio: In care proceedings the standard of proof is the balance of probabilities with cogent evidence required for serious findings; medical evidence of multiple injuries on separate occasions combined with the father's sole presence at collapse and dishonesty supports identifying him as perpetrator of prior and fatal abuse.
legal_issues: Whether C suffered non-accidental injuries on multiple occasions and who inflicted them
Whether Dr Johnson's LCR/reflux theory explained the fatal collapse
Whether threshold under section 31 was met for S and BL
Appropriate care orders and contact arrangements given findings
linked_authorities: Re H and R (Children) [1996] 1 FLR 80

confidence.notes: Very long medical fact-finding judgment; core findings and care order disposition are clear.

notes: Section 109(5)(h) life sentence quashed; 14-year determinate term substituted per Benfield.

enrichment.short_title: R v Hylands: section 109 firearm possession and automatic life sentence
key_facts: Hylands was convicted of a 2000 robbery in police uniform involving Murphy with a sawn-off shotgun and lump hammer; DNA and fingerprints linked him to the scene.
He had a 1990 conviction for robbery and wounding with intent, triggering section 109 mandatory life imprisonment for the second serious offence.
The indictment contained no separate firearm count and he did not admit possession during the robbery, though the facts were undisputed at trial.
The trial judge imposed life imprisonment with a notional 14-year determinate term; the Court of Appeal applied Benfield and Sobers.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against automatic life sentence under section 109 following robbery conviction.
enrichment.outcome: Life sentence set aside and replaced with 14 years' imprisonment, the determinate term the judge would otherwise have imposed.
enrichment.ratio: Where section 109(5)(h) applies, a second robbery offence is a serious offence only if firearm possession during the robbery is unequivocally admitted or specifically found by the jury; implied findings from joint venture facts or sentencing remarks are insufficient following Benfield, Eubank and Murphy.
legal_issues: Whether joint possession of a firearm during robbery must be admitted or specifically verdicted for section 109(5)(h)
Application of Benfield and Sobers, Eubank and Murphy to sentencing facts
Whether trial judges may find possession for section 109 without a Newton hearing or extra count
Appropriate determinate substitute sentence
linked_authorities: R v Benfield and Sobers [2004] 1 Cr App R 8
R v Eubank [2001] EWCA Crim 891
R v Murphy [2002] EWCA Crim 1324
R v Flamson [2001] EWCA Crim 3030

confidence.notes: Court of Appeal judgment focused on section 109(5)(h) procedure with clear outcome.

notes: GOC serious misconduct finding quashed on appeal; isolated negligence insufficient.

enrichment.short_title: Threlfall v GOC: optician discipline for inadequate retinal examination
key_facts: Mrs Threlfall, an ophthalmic optician, saw a patient with sudden large floater and possible retinal detachment on 12 July 2002 but did not dilate the pupil or perform a visual field test.
She referred the patient to Wigan Eye Unit for the next day; he attended A&E the same evening and underwent retinal detachment surgery.
The GOC Disciplinary Committee found inadequate examination and record-keeping proven and imposed a £500 penalty for serious professional misconduct.
The patient survived with sight saved, but the Committee found her examination fell seriously below professional standards.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal under section 23 of the Opticians Act 1989 from a GOC disciplinary decision.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed and the Disciplinary Committee's finding of serious professional misconduct quashed; isolated negligent omissions on favourable fact findings did not meet the seriousness threshold.
enrichment.ratio: An optician must use reasonable skill and care and perform clinically necessary additional examinations; failure to dilate or test visual fields when referring a suspected retinal detachment may be negligent, but on an isolated incident against an unblemished career the Disciplinary Committee's inadequately reasoned findings did not justify serious professional misconduct.
legal_issues: Scope of an optician's duty when referring a patient with suspected retinal detachment
Whether failure to dilate or perform visual field tests amounted to serious professional misconduct
Adequacy and timeliness of Disciplinary Committee reasons and Article 6 requirements
Distinction between negligence and serious professional misconduct on a single incident
linked_authorities: Preiss v General Dental Council [2001] UKPC 36
Ghosh v General Medical Council [2001] UKPC 29
Rao v GMC (PC Appeal No 21 of 2002)
Silver v GMC (PC Appeal No 66 of 2002)

confidence.notes: Burnton's judgment carefully distinguishes negligence from serious misconduct; some Committee fact findings ambiguous.

notes: Defra section 423 claim succeeds; limited counterclaim damages for unauthorised FMD burials and saddlery.

enrichment.short_title: Defra v Feakins: foot-and-mouth powers, section 423 and farm counterclaim
key_facts: Foot and mouth disease was diagnosed at Hill Farm in February 2001; MAFF/Defra slaughtered 937 animals and undertook cleansing and disposal operations on the infected place.
Defra claimed Kevin Feakins' transfer of the farm to Georgina Hawkins was a section 423 transaction defrauding creditors including IBAP's judgment debt.
Miss Hawkins counterclaimed for trespass and negligence over burial pits, lagoon, ash pit disposals and formaldehyde damage to saddlery.
Hart J upheld the section 423 claim but found most counterclaim allegations failed save limited unauthorised burials and negligent fogging damage.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court Chancery trial of Defra's section 423 claim and defendants' counterclaim arising from 2001 FMD operations.
enrichment.outcome: Section 423 claim succeeded with charging order relief to restore Defra's position; counterclaim partially succeeded with removal orders, user damages and £9,000 for saddlery but most alleged statutory trespasses failed.
enrichment.ratio: A post-judgment transfer of farm title to defeat creditors may be set aside under section 423; FMD statutory powers authorised most Defra operations on an infected place but burial in the C&D and Ash pits without power was trespass, and formaldehyde fogging negligently damaged leather goods despite lawful disinfection.
legal_issues: Whether the farm transfer to Miss Hawkins was a section 423 transaction at an undervalue to defraud creditors
Scope of statutory powers to bury, cleanse and store materials on an infected place during FMD
Whether TSE and groundwater constraints invalidated Defra's disposal methods
Quantum of user damages and compensation for unauthorised burials and saddlery damage
linked_authorities: Jaggard v Sawyer [1995] 1 WLR 269
Marcic v Thames Water Utilities [2003] UKHL 66

confidence.notes: Very long judgment; principal claim and counterclaim headline conclusions are clear though detail is extensive.

notes: Permission to appeal granted on abandonment and adverse possession arguments; stay ordered.

enrichment.short_title: Cook v Bates: driveway right of way, garage encroachment and permission to appeal
key_facts: Miss Cook bought No 13 Blakeston Road and sought removal of Mr Bates' garage encroaching about 0.25m over the boundary and a pedestrian-only gate blocking vehicular access along the shared driveway.
Transfers from the council granted reciprocal general rights of way over each half of the driveway between Nos 13 and 15.
Mr Bates said former owner Mr Hall agreed in the 1970s to the garage position and gate; the recorder held the boundary followed Land Registry plans and rights of way remained.
Bates applied out of time for permission to appeal, arguing abandonment of vehicular access and adverse possession.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to the Court of Appeal for permission to appeal and extension of time against a county court boundary and easement order.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal granted with expedited hearing; extension of time allowed despite 67-day delay; stay of removal orders pending appeal.
enrichment.ratio: Where a neighbour's long-standing garage encroachment and pedestrian gate may have coexisted with an informal agreement and non-use of vehicular rights, arguable issues of abandonment of the easement and adverse possession to the encroachment justify granting permission to appeal even after significant delay.
legal_issues: Whether the vehicular right of way over the driveway had been abandoned
Whether Mr Bates acquired possessory title by adverse possession to the garage encroachment area
Whether proprietary estoppel arises from Mr Hall's alleged agreement
Whether extension of time and a stay should be granted given litigation delay

confidence.notes: Interlocutory permission judgment; substantive issues identified but not finally decided.
